account: UNEP's Methane Alert and Response System (MARS) combines data from more than 30 satellite instruments with expert analysis and AI models. UNEP's case document on Hassi Messaoud, Algeria, records a Landsat 5 detection of methane at the site dated 1 July 1987. It counts 113 plumes since 1987 and estimates total emissions at 960,000 tonnes. Carbon Mapper's public catalog independently records that NASA's EMIT instrument saw methane plumes at the site on 17 dates from 17 August 2022 to 29 September 2024, at about 2,100 to 3,600 kilograms per hour. The case document attributes the emissions to an unlit flare caused by a passing valve on the flare line. The operator corrected the valve and restored normal operations. In October 2024 UNEP's International Methane Emissions Observatory confirmed mitigation of the source through MARS. UNEP states that no further emissions have been detected at the location since 15 October 2024. The Carbon Mapper catalog lists no later plume at that point. UNEP issued the case document in November 2024, according to the repository record, and the PDF's last-updated field reads 15 October 2024. UN News reported on 23 July 2026 that the Algerian alert led to the repair of a leak that had persisted for decades. On 31 August 2026 The Guardian reported that the leak, which had run for almost 40 years, was stemmed. The Guardian gave no data of its own on the site.

ai_role.statement: UNEP IMEO both developed and operates MARS (developer and deployer are the same body). UNEP's MARS page describes detection using more than 30 satellite instruments coupled with expertise and advanced AI models. The MARS FAQ says deep learning models monitor high-resolution satellite data for further emissions. The case document's boilerplate says MARS combines 30+ satellite instruments with expert analysis and AI models. None of these states which step in this case was AI-driven. The repair was carried out by the operator. The two case-document items are treated as a public body's official reports rather than vendor material.

UN News relays the UN's own account. Carbon Mapper's catalog draws on NASA's EMIT instrument and comes from a nonprofit outside the list of the system's partners.

fields.account: UNEP's Methane Alert and Response System (MARS) combines data from more than 30 satellite instruments with expert analysis and AI models. UNEP's case document on Hassi Messaoud, Algeria, records a Landsat 5 detection of methane at the site dated 1 July 1987. It counts 113 plumes since 1987 and estimates total emissions at 960,000 tonnes. Carbon Mapper's public catalog independently records that NASA's EMIT instrument saw methane plumes at the site on 17 dates from 17 August 2022 to 29 September 2024, at about 2,100 to 3,600 kilograms per hour. The case document attributes the emissions to an unlit flare caused by a passing valve on the flare line. The operator corrected the valve and restored normal operations. In October 2024 UNEP's International Methane Emissions Observatory confirmed mitigation of the source through MARS. UNEP states that no further emissions have been detected at the location since 15 October 2024. The Carbon Mapper catalog lists no later plume at that point. UNEP issued the case document in November 2024, according to the repository record, and the PDF's last-updated field reads 15 October 2024. UN News reported on 23 July 2026 that the Algerian alert led to the repair of a leak that had persisted for decades. On 31 August 2026 The Guardian reported that the leak, which had run for almost 40 years, was stemmed. The Guardian gave no data of its own on the site.
fields.summary: An alert from the UN Environment Programme's Methane Alert and Response System led an Algerian operator to fix an unlit flare at Hassi Messaoud; satellites show no emissions since 15 October 2024.

echoes.setting: Kazakhstan (KAZ_S_136, 43.39767°, 52.49505°; no place name given): gas pipeline leak first detected September 2025 (plume imaged by DLR's EnMAP 29 October 2025); operator transferred the gas flow to another pipeline, mitigation reported 26 November 2025; no further emissions detected since 12 March 2026 (document last updated 15 April 2026), but IMEO observed subsequent emissions at the location as of 21 May 2026
Argentina oil and gas facility: UNEP press release says the company fixed the leak after a MARS alert and satellite monitoring confirmed cessation
Alberta, Canada: trade-press report of UNEP's monthly snapshot describing a 175-tonne-per-week plume fixed by repairing a failed ball valve on pigging equipment (month only; first day used)

must_hold: A responsive focal point or operator. UN News reports only 13 percent of alerts lead to any response
Verification depends on later satellite coverage. The Kazakhstan case shows emissions can recur after confirmed mitigation
produced_by: Satellite detection and expert quantification of a large point source, followed by a MARS notification to the government and operator
An operator able to identify a simple equipment fault (passing valve on a flare line) and correct it

purpose: Satellite-based detection and notification of major methane emission events to governments and operators to enable mitigation.

ratings.reason: No identifiable individuals are documented as affected by the repair.
The operator fixed a passing valve on a flare line and restored normal operations at one facility, per UNEP's case document.

A source that UNEP traces to 1987 stopped emitting. Carbon Mapper's EMIT data show that it released about 2,100 to 3,600 kilograms of methane per hour in 2022 to 2024. No study quantifies the emissions avoided.
